utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, kindly call the cases.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Thursday, 27th of November, 2008. Good morning, Mr. Mundis, good morning, Mr. Dutertre, and good morning to your team. Good morning, Mr. Seselj. And I greet Madam Registrar, the usher, and all the people assisting us. We have a witness scheduled for today. He is available to be heard, if I am correct. Mr. Prosecutor, you will need basically one hour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can do it in 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. So Mr. Seselj will have an equal amount of time for his cross-examination, so that after the witness has been heard, the Trial Chamber can deal with decisions to be handed down -- or already handed down. In this way, Mr. Seselj will know what the situation is with regard to deadlines, about translations for decisions that can take a couple of days, so we'll have to do our level best for everybody to be best informed. Let's have the witness brought in, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Please state your first name, your last name, and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Ljubisa Vukasinovic. I was born on the 15th of August, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a current occupation? If so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an officer. I have the rank of colonel. I'm retired since -- I'm now retired, so I provide security for certain facilities. I work in the security business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, have you had an opportunity to testify in trials on the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia? If so, before which Court, in which case did you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have testified before, three times in Belgrade in the Ovcara trial. So these were repeated trials. I was there in 2003, 2004 and, I think, 2007. I gave statements to the investigating judge in Novi Sad in 2003, I think it was. I gave the first statement in 1998 to the military prosecutor in Belgrade. And I also gave a statement -- or, rather, testified as a Defence witness in the trial against Milos Sljivancanin in The Hague in 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have already testified in The Hague in the so-called Vukovar trial in 2006, and who were you a witness for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Were you a Prosecution or a Defence witness in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a witness of the Prosecution with respect to a criminal report filed against the people on trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as I understand it, you were a Prosecution witness in the Belgrade trial on the events in Ovcara, and here you were a Defence witness for Sljivancanin in the so-called Vukovar trial. Well, this enables me to ask you the following question. Over the last few years, at any point in time did anybody approach you to tell you to testify in favour of a given person, or did this never happen, unless or except when you were asked to meet with a Prosecutor or Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the period since my testimony in 2006, nobody contacted me from the Prosecutor's office. I learnt that I would be a Prosecution witness from a colleague of mine, General Delic, who's retired, and I learned that sometime in 2007, who rang me up and told me -- or, rather, asked me whether I knew that, and I said I did not. So he told me that I would be a Prosecution witness, and he showed me his investigation number and warned me that I should state my views in the matter. We talked, and I said that I was not aware of that, and I said I did not wish to be a Prosecution witness. Then, at his initiative, I wrote a statement which I had certified in the court, and I assume you have that verified certified statement. So after that time, there was a lull, a pause. Nothing happened until August of this year, when they called me up again -- or, rather, that same colleague called me up again to tell me that I was still on the list of Prosecution witnesses and that I ought to write a statement again. I did, indeed, write another statement, certified it in a court and sent it on, and I assume it arrived here. But despite that intervention, for the first time I received an invitation from the Municipal Court in Belgrade sometime in September. I was brought the summons by a courier, and it said that I should report to the office of The Hague Tribunal in Belgrade. That was a Friday, I believe, in September. I did report to The Hague Tribunal's offices in Belgrade, and I talked to Pale in the presence of his lawyer. I gave a brief interview. When I was asked whether I wanted to be a Prosecution witness, I still refused and said I didn't want to be a Prosecution witness, and stated my reasons. I said why I didn't want to testify. But that's where it ended. He said that I had to come if the Trial Chamber sends a summons. And I said that in that case, I would accept. I know what the sanctions would be if I acted otherwise. And that's where the whole thing ended. Now, a few days ago, I received a summons from the Trial Chamber. I received that, and here I am. So that's the entire process, from the beginning to the present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you did well to come. An additional question. You were a Prosecution witness in Belgrade. Why not be a Prosecution witness in The Hague? Why did you tell the Prosecutor that you didn't want to testify for him, since you'd already been a Prosecution witness? Do you have a special reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the main reason is that I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer? There was a break in communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I apologise for interrupting you, but there was a short technical problem. Could you please repeat your last answer. Just start all over again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had asked you why you had agreed to be a Prosecution witness in Belgrade but not here in The Hague. And you'd started with your answer, but there was a technical hitch, so please begin again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is the following: I started testifying in Belgrade because it was about the defence of positions and principles that were in the interests of my unit and my superiors. So I was a part of that process, a link in the chain, and therefore I could testify because I was defending my own unit and his officers, whereas I don't see my place and role in this trial. I don't see how I can contribute to the proceedings against Vojislav Seselj. I had no contacts with Dr. Vojislav Seselj at all, nor did I know him at all. At that time, I was an officer. As I said, I had the rank of major. I had nothing to do with the party, or any parties, and Mr. Seselj was a party leader and a politician. So in that context, I don't think I have any need to testify in this trial against Vojislav Seselj. I don't see my place and role in these proceedings, in this trial at all. So that's the substance of it, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have provided your argument. Prosecutor, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. Briefly, two things. Could Mr. Vukasinovic be more specific when speaking about General Delic? Is he speaking about Rasim or Bozidar Delic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have a lot of Delics and a lot of generals bearing that name. Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Bozidar Delic. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but my colleague was reminding me that he has to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, well, we can do that now. But as to the issue whether the witness was willing to come voluntarily as a Prosecution witness, and I'm referring back to what he said just now, there was indeed an interview back in September, on the 12th of September, 2008, with Mr. Vukasinovic. It was recorded, and Mr. Seselj received a copy of the recording. The question put to the witness was as follows: [In English] " ... would call you as a witness in the Seselj case. What do you do?" [Interpretation] I'll start again, because the beginning was this: [In English] "As a witness in the Seselj case, what do you do?" [Interpretation] The answer was as follows: [In English] "No problem. I will respond to the summons, but I think they are useless expenses, because I already said whatever I know."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let everything be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to put the question to you, Colonel. Can you confirm that on the 12th of September, 2008, you were asked by the Prosecutor whether you could be a witness in the Seselj case, and you answered what the Prosecutor has just read out; namely, that it was no problem for you, but you could see no point in it? Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the 12th of September, I was in the offices of The Hague Tribunal, and there was a 15-minute interview, so that is correct. But there are more reasons which I stated, which the gentleman didn't read out a moment ago. I gave my reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speak up, please, because it's difficult for the interpreters to hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was in the offices of The Hague Tribunal on the 12th. That is correct. And it's true that I said that my involvement as a Prosecution witness was useless, but I stipulated the reasons for which I didn't want to testify, and those reasons weren't read out a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, Judges, Mr. Vukasinovic was interviewed by The Hague investigators on the 26th of November, 2002, and The Hague Tribunal had planned that Mr. Vukasinovic be a witness in the Mrksic, Radic and Sljivancanin trial. And then The Hague Tribunal gave up on Mr. Vukasinovic's testimony, it changed its mind. When The Hague Tribunal decided not to call Mr. Vukasinovic as a witness, the Defence of Colonel Veselin Sljivancanin contacted him and proposed that he be a Defence witness. So as a man who had given a statement to the Prosecution beforehand and the Prosecution gave up on calling him, he became a Defence witness. Up until September this year, The Hague Tribunal, The Hague Prosecutor's office never, ever told him that he was planned as a witness in my trial, and for six years his name has been on the witness list. In the meantime, Mr. Vukasinovic gave two statements to my associates in which he expressly stated that he wished to be a Defence witness, and he also gave his views as to certain -- about certain circumstances. You have those statements. And when he gave those statements to my associates, The Hague Prosecutors turned up and asked him to be a Prosecution witness. That is quite obviously a play for witnesses, trying to seize the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I do indeed have your statement of the 16th to the 26th of November, 2008, before me, and towards the end -- or 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that towards the end of this statement, it was indicated that this interview was heard with a view to having you as a witness in the Vukovar trial. But then you were not called as a Prosecution witness in that trial and, if I understood properly, the Defence for Major Sljivancanin approached you as a potential witness, and you were a witness. And, furthermore, Mr. Seselj's associates asked you for some statements. As to the latter point, when, approximately, were you called by Mr. Seselj's associates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I met General Delic, Bozidar Delic, for the first time -- I think it was on the 18th. Well, you have it in the statement. I think it was the 18th of September or the 17th of September, 2007, in his office. So that was in December [as interpreted] 2007. That was the first time. And then we discussed it. And then in August 2008, I wrote another statement, and we met again in his office in the Assembly of Serbia, the National Assembly of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in September 2007, you met with General Delic, and in August 2008, you gave a statement. And it is in September 2008 that you were contacted by the OTP. Therefore, if I'm not wrong, between November 2002 and September 2008, the OTP had no contact with you. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, we could of course try to give the whole history of contacts with the witness, and then we could move to the testimony, but I want to react, if I may, to a comment by Mr. Seselj. He said that the OTP is trying to take, by force, witnesses from the Defence. You can be a Prosecution witness in one case and a Defence witness in another, and, at any rate, there was at least one contact between 2002 and 2008 with this witness, because, for instance, he was contacted in 2005 in relation to his possible testimony, and then he stated very clearly that he would be a Prosecution witness, as I said. And let me return to the fact that on page 7, line 5, the question put to him about the recording in September 2008, that was if the OTP calls you, it's still not recorded in the transcript. It was very clear, "If you were to be called by the Prosecution, what would you do?" And he said, "No problem, I would comply with the summons," he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is by way of a preliminary issue in order to shed the light --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on your testimony. I'd like to explain this to you. What matters to me is that you testify to what happened in Vukovar. That's what is the most important thing to me, and this is the reason why I'm going to ask you to take the solemn declaration. Yes, what did you want to add, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to what Mr. Dutertre just said, the witness is a professional officer. He's not a lawyer. He doesn't know the finesses of law, especially not trial law. He was called by The Hague Tribunal in Belgrade, and you know the terrible scarecrow image of The Hague Tribunal in The Hague. Now, although he gave statements for my Defence, the Prosecutor asked is he going to come. The witness says, "Yes," and the witness told you a moment ago that he was conscious -- fully conscious of the consequences if he didn't respond to the summons from the Prosecutor. Otherwise, he'd be arrested like Ljubisa Petkovic, or goodness knows what. And so in order to avoid sanctions, he said, the witness said, "No problem, I'll come, I'll come in if I have to." He didn't have counsel present, and nobody instructed him as to what he could or could not do. If he said, "I don't want to talk to you," and slammed the door, the Prosecutor couldn't do anything to him. But the witness did not know, nobody advised him that that's something that he could do, so the witness travelled here and from August to today I don't think my Defence had any contacts with him, exert any pressure on him or anything like that. And when he heard that he -- we heard that he would be coming, we wielded no influence on him. And that's how things stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the reason why I'd asked him initially in what circumstances he could have been contacted or not. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, briefly, and maybe we could move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you could decide whether it's good to have private session or not, if it's in the interest of witness, but I'd like to react to what was just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remind everybody of the fact that I am interested only in what happened in Vukovar. The rest is just light-years away from me. Madam Registrar, let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, part of what you stated on the 12th of September, 2008, was repeated in private session. Would you be against this being disclosed, being made public? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need. It can be made public. But I'd like to ask the Prosecutor to read everything I said, because he's just pulling excerpts out of context. I stated three or four reasons specifically why I did not wish to testify, whereas he's only quoting the last reason. And I think -- I don't think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please give these three reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first reason, as I said, was that I testified as a Defence witness in the case against Veselin Sljivancanin, and I said everything I was able to say about my place and role and the events in the matter of taking out the wounded people from the hospital, and I can only repeat what I said before. I have nothing new to say. That was my first reason. Secondly, I said that I had been a Defence witness, and now I think it doesn't make sense for me to appear as a Prosecution witness, to be a Defence witness in one trial and a Prosecution witness in another trial regarding the same events. Furthermore, a witness appearing as a Prosecution witness, as an officer who is highly respected in the town where I live, is something that is not appropriate. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, we have spoken long enough about your being called here as a witness for the Prosecution or for the Defence, but I wish to remind you that once you have entered your solemn declaration, you are a witness in the hands of this Court, and the only thing we want you to do is to tell the truth, to the best of your knowledge, and to give accurate answers to the questions that are put to you by the Prosecution and by the Defence, and to do so truthfully and wholly. So what I'm saying is that once you have entered your solemn declaration, the issue of whether you appear as a witness for one or the other party is simply irrelevant. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes. That's not a problem. I don't know why all this discussion. I'm here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I must inform you that Prosecutor Max Moore, in the trial of Mrksic, Radic and Sljivancanin, during the cross-examination of Mr. Ljubisa Vukasinovic, told him the following: "I suggest that you're a first-class bad person who has come here to protect yourself."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. You are going too fast. The interpreters can't follow you. Please repeat what you are reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I suggest that you are a first-class scoundrel and that you have, in fact, come here to protect not only yourself, but others, and to make a statement which suits their purpose." This indicates what the OTP in The Hague thinks of the eminent Colonel Ljubisa Vukasinovic. Let me tell you the following, without interruption. Something similar happened in the Limaj et al case. Those were the three Albanians who were tried for war crimes, and the two chief accused were acquitted. And in the case of Slobodan Milosevic, a policeman came to testify, and he testified about the crimes committed by Limaj and others, and then the Prosecutor suggested to Mr. Milosevic, he said, "So-and-so is here. He might be of interest for Mr. Milosevic, so we are telling him he can talk to him and call him as a Defence witness if he likes." And then Mr. Milosevic spoke to this man. He was the chief of a police station in Prizren, I think, I can't remember his name now, but it's reliable information, and he testified as a Defence witness for Mr. Milosevic. And Jeffrey Nice, during the cross-examination, used the same arguments that Limaj's Defence used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Milosevic case is totally irrelevant here, but when it comes to what you quoted from the statement of the Prosecutor in the Vukovar case, that may have some relevance. I would have a comment to make on that. Mr. Dutertre, you wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just wanted to say that we -- Mr. Seselj seems to have started his cross-examination. Judge Harhoff said something that I wanted to say, myself. The witness has come here to tell the truth, so I do not see what the problem is. I would respectfully request that we start the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm going to ask you to take the solemn declaration, but first I've heard something that I was not aware of. Is it true that in the Vukovar case, you were called a scoundrel by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true. My lawyer translated this to me later, and then he apologised before the second round of talks, he apologised in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's something I must add, Mr. President. The Prosecutor did not actually apologise. He was attacked by the Defence counsel, so he tried to mitigate his standpoint, but he did not utter the word "apology." I have read the entire transcript in detail. Mr. Vukasinovic probably hasn't seen it, but I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, you see, I was right to start this hearing at 8.30, because we've been sitting for 40 minutes and you haven't yet read the solemn declaration. But please do so now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may be seated. Witness, you may be seated. I believe that my fellow Judge has two questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are now under oath, so I expect you to tell the truth. I wanted two clarifications from you. You referred to two statements that were allegedly certified before a court. I'm not sure. You may be referring to a signature that was certified by a court. And you said that you sent that to the Tribunal. Who did you send that to, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certified those statements in the 4th Municipal Court in Belgrade. I certified my first and last name and my statement, and then a copy of the statement remains in the court and the other copies are mine. I gave them to General Bozidar Delic and his Defence brought those statements here, probably. I didn't send them by mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. The other question I have for you refers to the statement you gave to the OTP. I may be mistaken, but I thought that you said that when you gave your statement in November 2002, the OTP team told you that you were expected to testify in the Sljivancanin case, and that, therefore, you did not expect to have to testify in the Seselj case. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 2002, as you say, I gave a statement about the circumstances in Vukovar. That was a long time ago, and nobody mentioned my testimony. I just made a statement about what had happened in Vukovar and at the end it said that the statement could be used before the ICTY in trials, in trial proceedings. It didn't say against whom. And then when the trial started, I appeared as a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. That's exactly what I was expecting of you. One more thing. On two or three occasions, you have said here that you have nothing new to tell us, but you have to understand that here the evidence is received in the courtroom, so even if you have nothing to add on top of what you stated in previous testimonies, it makes sense for you to come back and testify in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me give you some explanation. Of course, you're familiar with the way we proceed in this Tribunal, but let me repeat it. The Prosecutor will put a number of questions to you, based on a statement you gave to the OTP, and it's quite possible that the Prosecutor will show you a number of documents. The three Judges sitting before you will probably put questions to you, considering your functions within the JNA. The accused in this case, Mr. Seselj, will conduct his cross-examination and also put questions to you. Afterwards, we may go on to redirect by the Prosecution. If we all play our part correctly, the hearing should run very smoothly to help us ascertain the truth, because that's our main purpose here, the purpose of everyone. Mr. Dutertre, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Colonel, let's now deal with what you know, what you saw, because that's what is relevant for the Trial Chamber today. First question, related to what I would call your personal background, first question: Where were you between September and November 1992 [as interpreted]? It's not "1992," as it's stated on the transcript; it's 1991.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you. I was an officer of the Guards Brigade, deployed in the security department of the Guards Brigade as assistant of chief of security for staff affairs, and around the 1st of September I was undergoing training, regular two-year training. And then my training was interrupted on the 15th of September. I reported to the Guards Brigade, and as of the 29th I set out with the Guards Brigade to carry out a combat task unblocking the barracks in Vukovar and liberating the barracks in Vukovar from the Croatian authorities. So on the 29th of September, I was in Vukovar. After that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I don't have all the time in the world. I will put questions to you, and you will be able to provide additional information. Until when did you stay in Vukovar with the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I returned on the 24th of November, 2001 -- 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but something is not quite clear to me. The Prosecutor asked you until when you remained in Vukovar, and you answer that you returned there. What is relevant for us here is to know until when you remained in Vukovar as a military person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the 23rd. And on the 24th, in the morning, I returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the 23rd of November, 1991, you remained in Vukovar until that time. And on the 24th, you left for Belgrade. Okay, now it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The date of arrival and the date of departure are not necessarily the same things. Who was your immediate superior in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: In Vukovar, for a time I was under Veselin Sljivancanin, from the 29th of September to the 4th of November, 1991, when I was his operations officer in the security organ. On the 4th of November, 1991, the commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion fell ill, and Mrksic appointed me commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion, where I was also the commander of the Negoslavci command post. And from that date until the 23rd of November, I was under the command of Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay, it's very clear. Let me conclude on the description of your activities between September and November. Okay, I've concluded, and now I'm going to move on to a very specific day, and I have the following question for you. Where did you go on the 20th of November, 1991, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, 1991, at 0600 hours in the morning, I was given a task by Major Sljivancanin. I was told to come to the hospital area with some buses. So it was 0600 hours in the morning of the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. So you arrived there at the hospital at 6.00 a.m. on November 20th. Why were you asked to go there with buses? What was the purpose of this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: The task given me by Veselin Sljivancanin was to come there with buses to evacuate the prisoners from the hospital to the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. Whom did you see, apart from the prisoners or, rather, the persons that were at the hospital? Whom did you see amongst Serb forces at the hospital on that particular morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: The forces of the Vukovar Territorial Defence. You can't talk about Serb forces. There were forces of the Vukovar Territorial Defence. Well, "forces." It was a group of men who were there in the barracks -- in the hospital, that is. They were there, their commanders were there, Miodrag Vujovic, Stanko Vujanovic, and Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni. Those were their detachment commanders and they were there with a group of fighters. Major Sljivancanin was there also and some other officers from my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, the Prosecutor is dealing with a point of paramount importance. We have to be extremely cautious now. You were the commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion. Your task was to go -- from what you say, was to go and fetch prisoners at the hospital. This is the military task that was entrusted to you as a JNA officer, and at the time the JNA was an army -- an armed forces that was enjoying a very good reputation in the world. As such, as a JNA officer, did you take with you enough military policemen to carry out this task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my assessment, there were enough, because from the hospital to the barracks there is only a short distance, only two or three kilometres. It's not a long march.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many military policemen did you have with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military policemen, two in every bus, and in the barracks there was a military police company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, 12, 12 MPs. And to guard how many prisoners? How many prisoners were you supposed to guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know the number at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, how can you conduct a task if you don't have the necessary information, because you're telling me that you had no idea. Let's assume that you are told to go and fetch a number of prisoners, and you find that there are 3.000 prisoners. You can't conduct that task with just 12 MPs. So you had no information about this? You're here to tell us the truth. If mistakes were made, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know the precise number, but it wasn't I who selected the buses or the soldiers. It was all organised by the brigade logistics. I simply took over the buses with the soldiers and came to the place I was ordered to come to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many buses were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were six buses and two policemen in each one, and my Pugh vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So the logistics unit of the brigade sent six buses, and you, without knowing how many prisoners there would be, you decide to assign two policemen per bus. Fine. We may proceed, because now we know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just one point of clarification. Page 21, line 18, the transcript is incomplete. I suppose it's going to be corrected later on. But from what I heard in the French translation, I believe that the witness stated that Lancuzanin, Kameni, was present at the hospital. It has not been recorded on the English transcript. I suppose it will be corrected later on, but I'm raising that point because I have a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned the names of three individuals at the hospital, Stanko Vujanovic, Vujovic and Kameni. How well did you know these people before? Did you have professional dealings with these people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that I knew them especially well, but I can't say that I didn't know them, either. While I was the operations officer, and when I toured the assault detachments, and that was the 1st Assault Detachment at the -- where I attended briefings, and I saw Milan [Realtime transcript read in error "General"] ^ Lancuzanin at those briefings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've just given us a very relevant piece of information. You have stated something about briefings in relation to future operations. What about this task, this task of going and fetching prisoners at the hospital; had it been part of -- or subject of a briefing earlier on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not attend the briefing, but most probably this was discussed at the briefing held by the commander, Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you did not attend that meeting. Is it customary? And the reason I'm putting that question to you is because I am familiar with rules. At the JNA, is it customary, when you're conducting a major-scale operation, is it normal, customary, for the head of the military police not to attend preparatory meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not normal, but I'll tell you why I didn't attend. It's not customary, but the battalion commander in this case was ill, and I was standing in for him. So I was more of a security organ, and the commander didn't call me to come at that point in time. My predecessor had attended the briefings before, but he felt that I was doing only a temporary assignment, which is why he didn't call me back. Major Sljivancanin was given the task of involving me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, now it's clear enough. You have to understand that we analyse everything you say on the basis of what we know about command rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be a problem in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Page 24, line 3, you mentioned General Lancuzanin. Is there a mistake? Did you actually say "General Lancuzanin," or did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Lancuzanin. Yes, that is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You said that you saw Kameni during those meetings. With regard to the other two people, Vujovic and Vujanovic that you mentioned, did you see them at those meetings as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I would see them less, but I did see them around. I wasn't there all the time. I was there from time to time, but when I was there, I did see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor's question is bound to raise a question with us. When you have these type of meetings, when the commanding officer of the Territorial Defence was present, all the other people attending such meetings. In military terms, and I'm speaking to a military man, does this mean that all -- that the entire meeting, the entire operation, is under the sole command, sole military command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the commander of the 1st Assault Battalion organised meetings every evening, and so he would call all his subordinate commanders and the commanders of the Territorial Defence, the two detachments that were under his commander. So everybody under his command would attend the meetings, and then he would set out plans for combat and operations the following day, and everybody was given his assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Colonel, on that morning, around 6.00 in the morning on the 20th of November, 1991, in the hospital, how would you describe the behaviour of Vujanovic, Vujanovic [as interpreted], Kameni and their soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That morning when I arrived, a large group of prisoners from the barracks had already been taken out along a ramp, a little wall, towards the entrance to the hospital. There's a sort of little wall, and they were standing there. Whether two-by-two or three-by-three, anyway, there was a group of people by the entrance check-point, and then the other group was by the buses, the TO Vukovar, and their commanders were there. And when I started to board the people up onto the bus, there was a lot of noise, there were threats, there were various comments made by those soldiers, but there was no aggressive behaviour or an aggressive atmosphere or anything. It was more verbal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have any recollection of the threats that were uttered then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly they would -- the threats would be -- actually, they recognised people in the group who were there, adversaries who had done some evil to them during July and August, that they had something against some of the people there, and nobody mentions that, because in July the Croatian forces committed crimes against the Serb population, and during the fighting people fell casualties. So they probably recognised all the people who'd done something bad to them and who were responsible earlier on. And when they saw that they had been captured and taken prisoner, they wanted to let them know and tell them that they would either -- they would say they'd beat them up, or get their own back, or things like that. That was the idea they had in mind. But we controlled the situation, and during that period of time there were no attacks there by the hospital. Later on, things came to a head in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I understand that you told the prisoners -- well, the people who were in the hospital, you told them to get into the buses. Once the prisoners were boarded onto the buses, I'm speaking about these people who were in the hospital, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I supervised the boarding of three buses, and since the people in the hospital conducted a triage, I went towards the barracks with those three buses. And in the barracks, I organised -- within the barracks compound, I left them there and organised security for them, because I had a police security company there, and they were given the task of providing security for the buses until I returned with the other group. Do you want me to tell you how it was? A group of TO members had already arrived in the barracks, so they were there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: We'll get to this point later. So you left with three buses towards the JNA barracks. Then there were TO people who were already there. Where did they come from, these TO people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: They were the people who -- well, from the hospital, they changed their direction. They followed me, followed the direction I took. They were the same people that had gathered in front of the hospital. Later on, they gathered in the barracks. They were all the same people, the same fighters from the Territorial Defence of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have two problems here. You will have -- you noted that the TO people were excited. I mean, they had insulted the prisoners, and this could have degenerated. And you noted that the TO people followed. So in the way you saw things then, since you had not been part of the meeting held the previous day by the Command, did you think that the TO people had been given a task for that purpose or did you believe that they had nothing to do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my opinion that they probably hadn't been given an assignment. I really can't say. All I do know is that while we were there, they couldn't do anything to those people, and those people were absolutely protected, properly protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But when you realised what the atmosphere was, why did you not call for some reinforcement, because I suppose that you had some means of communication. Why did you not call the Command in order to ask for reinforcement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't need it, any reinforcements. I had a military police company, and they provided security for all three buses. I had the right number of men to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's sum up. So you have -- in the buses, you have military police officers, but you've added that the police company was on the spot. How many men did you have there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military police company numbered about 65 soldiers at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Why didn't you ask these 65 men to go and help the TO people or clear them out of the way? Why was that not done? How many were there among these excited TO members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me explain it like this: The military police barracks and company had 65 men, as I told you. It provided that number of security in the barracks, and the others had 15 to 20 soldiers, the TO. But the barracks -- you couldn't throw them out. There were about 30 of them, 30 to 40 men, and you couldn't throw them out. There would be conflicts and clashes. But they were just standing there. They couldn't do anything to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you are saying that they couldn't do anything. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to ask this question about the number of people, but it's been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So you left the hospital with three buses. You got to the JNA barracks, where there are 30 to 40 TO members. What was the attitude of the TO members who had followed you from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was similar to the situation in front of the hospital. They kept making gestures with their hands. They swore, they expressed their anger. Some of them wanted to enter the building, but couldn't. That kind of thing. They couldn't enter because the doors were shut. The people were in the buses and the doors were shut, so all they could do was verbally abuse them. And they reacted to some of the people they saw in the buses and whom they recognised; not all of them. So this anger of theirs was expressed in brandishing weapons that they might have had in their hands, in swearing at the people, but no other attacks, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, a point of terminology. When you say or mention the Territorial Defence, does this, in your mind, encompass Petrova Gora or -- Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica? Do you clarify this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were people -- well, the same people from the town of Vukovar. The only thing is that they were divided into groups. And these are geographic names of Vukovar, parts of Vukovar, Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica, so they named their detachments according to the district in which they lived. But it's the same group of people that belonged to the TO of Vukovar, because these are places in Vukovar. But the commander -- the Petrova Gora Detachment commander was Stankovic, then Vujovic, and the commander of Leva Supoderica was Milan Lancuzanin. But they were all people from the same place, same locality, but they just gave their detachments different names of the different districts of one and the same town, Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: At that point in time when you got there, among those 30 to 40 men who were there, who were you able to identify, who in your recollection was present at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Milivoj Vujovic there. I didn't see Milan in the barracks, Milan Lancuzanin, I mean. Milivoj Vujovic, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you later on return to the hospital, and if you did, why did you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go back to the hospital, and the reason is this: I -- a courier brought me a list from Major Sljivancanin, saying that I should take 20 people back to the hospital, that I should find them in the buses, take them off the buses, and bring them back to the hospital. And then I was given a bus, and I tried to find those people. So I went from one bus to the next, called the names out. I found all these people. Well, there were some problems when I wanted to transport them -- transfer them in the bus. But, anyway, I did manage to get them out of the first buses, put them in the others, and take them to the hospital, where Mr. Sljivancanin, with the hospital staff and members of the TO Defence -- Milan Lancuzanin was there, anyway, and so was Milivoj Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic, Milivoj Vujovic, and they discussed what to do with the people. They were probably innocent, so at the intervention of the hospital and the hospital staff, and on the basis of the conversations they had, they let them go. So about 15 of these people were let go because they said they hadn't taken part in any combat activities, they were just people who happened to be in the hospital but weren't combatants. So it was at this intervention that they were released. Sljivancanin's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... follow-up questions. Here is the first one. You said that you got all these 20 people together, and you said, "Some people gave me problems." Who caused problems for you? And once you've answered this, I have another question.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, the members of the Territorial Defence who were present there were a bit difficult, because they thought we would take them all back. And then they asked us where we were going and what we were going to do with those 20 people. They were interested in where we would take them. And then I said we would take them back, and I suppose they were dissatisfied when they heard that and then they reacted. They reacted in the way they reacted. There was a lot of noise and a lot of swearing. They swore at me, they went that far, but we managed to take them off the buses and return them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. At the hospital, you said that there was a discussion between Vujovic, Vujanovic, Lancuzanin and Major Sljivancanin. What was the position of Vujovic, Vujanovic and Lancuzanin regarding certain prisoners? What did they say to Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to notice -- I can't tell you all the details, but, anyway, Sljivancanin, let me correct myself, he wasn't the commander, he was the chief of security, so this term "commander" is very often bandied about, but he was chief of security, not commander, in actual fact. Anyway, they were in favour of having these people released, because Major Sljivancanin consulted them, and they asked the people to be returned. And the hospital staff asked -- he asked the hospital staff whether these people deserved to be released, and they confirmed that, and they used their authority to prevail upon him, and he respected that. So, yes, they did play a part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I hadn't thought of this before, but now it appears that among the prisoners, broadly speaking, in the hospital, there was some 20 people whose names were on a list, and those people were released. So they left freely, if I understand you properly. Does this mean that you -- you were in charge of the mission and the operation you had been given. Does this mean that the other people who remained as prisoners were individuals who could be blamed for something? Because if I understand properly, the quote/unquote "innocents," these 15 to 20 people were let go, while the quote/unquote "culprits" were kept. Is that what you thought then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can't draw that kind of conclusion. As for these people, there was an intervention. They provided -- the people in the hospital provided a list. It wasn't Sljivancanin who thought this up. Now, as to the others, nobody intervened, but we were to establish that later on to see -- we had to see whether there was anybody responsible for the events, those who were responsible, who the combatants were. All that was to be determined at a later stage, because they were all in the same role. They were neither innocent, nor guilty. That was left to later on, to be established what their responsibility was in the Vukovar operation, because the fact remains that many people who did not wish to surrender and did have the chance of doing so had changed their clothing and entered the hospital to try to pull out of Vukovar that way with this disguise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you are saying. We've heard witnesses and we've seen documents. We therefore know that the people found in Ovcara, some of them were under age. For instance, there was somebody born in 1975, another in 1976, another in 1977, so there were people who were under age. But there was also -- they were also hospital staff members, and at a stretch one could think that, from what you say, that the people who were released were people who had nothing to do with what happened. So how do you account for the fact that we found, among the victims, people who were under age and staff members from the hospital? And they were not combatants, so how could that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that, Mr. President. I don't know that there were minors or hospital staff members. As far as I was concerned, these were people from the ages of 25 to 30. I don't know whether there were any under-age people, any minors, or any hospital staff, for that matter, because I didn't have any time to go into matters like that. All I was there to do was to take them in and to have them boarded up into the buses. I didn't go through them all to be able to confirm who was who. That was not something that I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When are we going to have the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to waste time on translations issues, but I have to mention this. I'd asked what was the position of Kameni, Vujovic and Vujanovic regarding some prisoners. This was on page 32, line 14 of today's transcript. The answer, as it appeared in the transcript, was this: [In English] "They were in favour of having these people released." [Interpretation] I believe -- I'm not sure, but I think I heard the opposite in French. They were not in favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you, Colonel, repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in favour of having those people released, and that's what they proposed, to have them released.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, everything's clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Vujovic, Vujanovic and Kameni were in favour of releasing the people on that list, on the famous list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once this was done, what did you do? Did you remain at the hospital, did you go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: When all that was over, the remainder of the people who were waiting, the prisoners who were waiting, I boarded them up into two buses, and the third bus, which was half empty and there were just five or six people who remained, we took the same direction and I transported them to the barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. And once -- what was the time when you got to the barracks, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: In my statements, I said that it was around 10.00. The first group, that was around 10.00. The second group, since you're asking me, that must have been sometime around 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. So return towards 12:00, midday, to the JNA barracks with three remaining buses, if I'm not wrong. And what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: What I saw was this: That the buses from the first group that I left behind at the barracks were not there anymore, and I asked the company commander of the military police, who was responsible there, where are the buses with the prisoners, and he said that an order had come from headquarters that they be transported. And an officer came by with a combat vehicle and drove them off to Ovcara, and the commander issued orders that, "You should go to Ovcara too," that is to say, me, "with the other group, the second group."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, regarding -- I've done some research on this in the meantime as to the position taken by Vujovic, Vujanovic and Kameni with regard to the 20 prisoners. So I've done some research, and I might want to refresh the witness's recollection with regard to a statement he gave in 2007 before a Belgrade court to see whether he can confirm now what he said. But I do not have any translation into English, so this is a very rough translation that I have in English. But we can look at the original B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: It seems that you said that Vujovic was at the hospital --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I demand that this be put on the overhead projector, because the Prosecutor's interpretation is quite impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a version, but it's marked and highlighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose you referred to the interview by the Presiding Judge of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But just to save time, I'm going to have a clean version of it, without any markings or annotations. Mr. Seselj is indeed right, it would be good to put it on the overhead projector, so I'll get to this later, once this is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be best to have the break now. It will give you time to prepare all this during the break. And it's nearly 10.00 anyway, so let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Dutertre, have you prepared the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a problem of translation from English into B/C/S. I do not need -- or B/C/S into English. I do not need to refresh the witness's memory after all. Can I be told how much time I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Colonel, before the break you told us that you were told to go to Ovcara with the three remaining buses, I suppose. Is that what you actually did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My three remaining buses, where I was, I took them to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Was this an order you had received?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was an order that I received indirectly. It was the order of the commander, which was conveyed to me by my company commander, Mladen Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Around what time did you arrive in Ovcara, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived at Ovcara at around 1300 or 1330. At around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you arrived there, had -- the three other buses you had seen at the hospital in the morning, had they already arrived?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first three buses that I had transferred earlier in the morning had already there and they were empty, and the prisoners had been moved to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw inside the hangar? What was the situation there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: As I approached the hangar, the facility that had been probably envisaged by our commanders, as I approached I saw that the buses were empty, and I was surprised. How come the buses were empty? I wondered where the people were. And as I got off the bus, I saw a group of people in front of the hangar, 30 to 40 of them. They were coming in, going out. I got off the bus, I entered the hangar, and I saw that they were all intermingled, the prisoners and the members of the TO. The hangar was open, and there were TO members inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In what state were the prisoners inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Since the hangar is quite large, they were split in little groups, and I could see injuries on them. There were occasional puddles of blood. I could see fear on their faces, I could see that some were bleeding from their arms or from their nose, so there were traces of physical violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you entered the hangar, did you see any members of the TO who were there, did you see any of them abusing the prisoners physically?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was a much smaller group. Most of them were in front of the hangar, and then a smaller group of 10 to 15 were inside, and they were talking to these people and chasing certain individuals around the hangar. And as they saw me, they halted. When I entered, I yelled at them, "What's going on," and I told them to stop whatever they were doing. At that moment, inside -- in front of the hangar, I saw Mr. Vujovic, and it occurred to me that I should ask his assistance to chase his people out of the hangar so I could ensure that the second batch of prisoners could enter the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Am I to understand that this was taking place, this maltreatment was taking place before Mr. Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Mr. Vujovic did not react at that moment against his people who were being violent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Let me go back in time a little. I'm not talking about the moment when you entered the hangar. I'm talking about the moment when you arrived with three buses at Ovcara, the last three buses. At that time, did you see any JNA officers there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a chief of staff, Lieutenant Colonel Panic, but only for a few seconds, as it were. I just saw him, I criticised him, and then he left. And then I saw soldiers of the military police from the 80th Brigade, which is to say that, yes, the policemen were there, they were present, and I didn't see anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, this was a critical moment. You were a witness of abuse of prisoners. Under such circumstances, pursuant to JNA rules, shouldn't the highest-ranking officer on the spot control the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Unfortunately, the highest-ranking officer moved away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but who was the highest-ranking officer who should have exercised control over the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation should have been under the control of the commander of the 80th Brigade, because that was his area of responsibility. And especially since his policemen were there, that was an indicator to me that somebody had already called him and that he had prepared military police to secure the hangar. And in this movement from the barracks to Ovcara, for me this was quite a surprise. This was quite an unknown for me. But when I arrived and when I saw the soldiers there and the military policemen, I realised that this had been agreed at the level of the Command and that the problem was solved, in the sense of this transfer, that this had been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. You are telling us that the situation should have been under the control of the commander of the 80th Brigade. Can you repeat his name, the name of this commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic. He was the commander of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade. I think Milorad Vojnovic. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he was not present, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the commander doesn't have to be present everywhere. He has his people, his subordinates, but this was his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, he was not there. If I understand properly, you were the highest-ranking officer in that building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I was a major, and there was Lieutenant Colonel Panic there. He was chief of staff. He was second in command after Commander Mrksic, and he was present, he was the highest-ranking officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, the command was held by Lieutenant Colonel Panic. Then you explain that he left, Lieutenant Colonel Panic left. You remained inside the hangar. I suppose that members of the TO continued mistreating prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take into account JNA command rules. Weren't you supposed to intervene then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, and I did intervene. I prevented further mistreatment by getting involved myself, by relying on my authority, by relying on the soldiers who were there and their commander. I threatened them, I chased these people out, and I ensured that the prisoners be left alone in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling us that you put an end to mistreatment and that you chased these people out. Are you talking about the TO members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The prisoners remained inside the building. The TO people were outside. What about the military policemen, did you position them around the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you instruct them to open fire if someone tried to enter the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that particular case, I wasn't able to issue such an order because I wasn't their superior, but I told them to carry out what the task of the military police is, because it was their responsibility to ensure that nobody came in, into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you tried to deal with the situation as best you could. But at that particular moment in time, did you have the necessary equipment to get in touch with your Command? Did you have a Motorola, did you have a radio transmitter, allowing you to get in touch with the HQ and Colonel Mrksic? Were you able to do this immediately or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have a Motorola, but I wasn't on-line with the commander because I wanted to put an end to the mistreatment and to ensure order and to go to the Command right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But considering the situation as it was, weren't you supposed, as an officer, to immediately call Colonel Mrksic or his deputy at the Command to report on the situation, to tell them about the steps you had just taken? Why is it that you didn't do it at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, there was no time for that, because my first instinct was to prevent any further mistreatment. And this is what guided me. You know, the commander always looks for a solution, because the commander would ask me, "What have you done so far," and then he would ask me, "What do you need?" Had I called him right away, he would have said, "Why are you calling me if you haven't done anything yourself?" So this is the procedure in the military. Up to a certain level, you can do something yourself, and then if need be, you can turn to your superior. And that was the reason why I didn't do it right away. I didn't want to react immediately in the sense that you are describing. And the other reason was that my superior was present there, and he left, or, rather, I assumed that he, as the second in command, left. And all of this had been taking place in his presence with the first group, when the major mistreatment took place, and I assumed that he would go to the commander and report on him about what had taken place. That's why I didn't call the commander, myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were also the head of the military police. Shouldn't you have ordered an investigation to try and find out who had abused the prisoners in order then to punish the authors? Was this part of your functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right. I couldn't immediately list the names of the people who had done that, but I did take certain measures. This question wasn't put to me by the Prosecutor. I guess he intended to do that. But I informed the commander, Mrksic, immediately, sometime at around 3.30. I informed him about the situation as it was there. I told him that I prevented further mistreatment and I told him that this could be repeated. Therefore, we needed to step up the security measures and to properly ensure security, in the police sense, so that the TO members would not be able to approach the hangar. He listened to me, and then he said, "You can go."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's on the record. At 3.30 p.m., you informed Colonel Mrksic about the situation. You told him that a number of prisoners had been mistreated and that security needed to be stepped up. And in answer to that, Colonel Mrksic told you that you could go. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Colonel, you've told us that you took a number of steps. Who else, amongst the members of Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica whom you know, who else from these people did you recognise at Ovcara on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I could only recognise their main people. Mr. Vujovic was there, for the most part, and he assisted me for a while, and then Kameni was there just very briefly, and also Stanko Vujanovic. So all three of them were at Ovcara at some point in time. I can't tell you how much time they spent there, but I can tell you that Vujovic was there for the longest period of time. While I was there, he was there too. However, all three of them were present at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Around what time did you leave Ovcara, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I left between 1500 and 1530.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. When you left, what about the members of Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica; were they still there? Can you tell us if they were still there when you left?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were there, but some had already left. They were there, but not that many of them. Out of those 30, 40 in total, at the time when I left Ovcara, there were only 15 to 20 remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you see the others leave with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them leave. Since this is quite a flat area, I saw them leave towards other buildings in Ovcara. I saw them leave in small groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. You saw them leave towards other buildings in Ovcara. You told Colonel Mrksic what was going on. It's a question I wanted to ask you, but you've already told us about this. When did you find out about the massacre of prisoners of Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about that -- well, was it on the following day or the day after? It was on the 21st or 22nd, at around that time, either 21st or 22nd, shortly thereafter. It was in the morning hours, as I was preparing to transfer my duties to somebody else. My brigade was getting ready to leave, and one of my assistants came and whispered to me about the rumours around the village; that people were gone, that they had disappeared, that they had probably been liquidated. He said to me something to that effect, and I took this with a grain of salt. I wasn't sure, I wasn't quite convinced. It didn't seem likely that something like that could have happened. And later on, I asked him, "Were you serious about this?" And he said, "Yes. I heard these rumours circulating in the village." So to tell you the truth, I couldn't react to his story. I didn't pay particular attention to what he was saying. I thought those were just rumours. I couldn't even assume that something like that could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: One last point. You told us that Kameni was there for a brief period of time; page 44, line 21. What did you mean by that, exactly? Did you see him briefly, did you see him leave? Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw him, but for a brief period of time. That would be the best description.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on the 20th or on the 21st, you heard this rumour, and am I to understand that you did nothing, yourself, afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the following days or months, did the military command order what is called a command investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At what point in time were you, yourself, summoned by an authority, whatever it is, to testify about these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998, for the first time. I testified at the military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998, which military tribunal was it, and it was a case against whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the case against unidentified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you interviewed by an investigative magistrate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Colonel Gojovic. He's currently a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So I suppose he asked you the same questions I'm asking you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There is a statement that I gave about those events, and later on there was a lull until the proceedings that started concerning Ovcara at the military court, and it was then we started giving statements to the prosecutor against very specific individuals, accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minor matter that may have escaped our attention. When you left the site, the situation was under control because the military policemen were around the building, but what about these military policemen; did they leave with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my policemen left with me, because this was taken over by the military police of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, the others stayed there? The ones from Kragujevac, they stayed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you reported the matter to Colonel Mrksic, when he told you that you could go, what was your feeling, what was your impression? Did you have the feeling that he was going to take the necessary steps or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
