utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll tell you my thoughts, since you are guiding me in that direction, and those were exactly my thoughts at the time. It wasn't clear to me, and knowing my commander, it wasn't clear to me how he reacted in that way to a very serious report that I gave him, a very serious report provided by me, especially knowing that we did not have such situations previously, where the commander wasn't reacting to something that was portrayed to him as negative, and he didn't tell me to go and resolve that. So thinking about that, I came to the conclusion that this was some kind of an arrangement between them. And later on, when I heard that there was a government session of the SOA Baranja and Western Srem, chaired by Mr. Goran Hadzic, where our representative from the Command was present, Lieutenant Colonel Panic, I learned that they had precisely discussed this, that Goran Hadzic said to Mrksic -- later on I put this all together, and I'm telling you now about what I heard later. And as a result of that, I came to a conclusion that this had been a decision and that it had been ordered for the prisoners to be turned over to them, because they had their own organs of authorities, and that they would try them. And I think that Goran Hadzic tricked our commander, so to speak, and that our commander gave them control over the prisoners, and this is what happened afterwards. These were my thoughts, and if one was to look at all of it, all of the aspects, then one would come to that conclusion, because it was not natural for the commander not to react to such a situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm going to try to summarise what you've said. It's just an assumption of yours, of course, but you're perfectly entitled to make assumptions. According to you, Goran Hadzic and Colonel Mrksic, as well as Colonel Panic, had reached an agreement with relation to the prisoners, to the way the prisoners should be guarded. According to you, there was an agreement between them, and your assumption is that when you found out about all this, you thought that Colonel Mrksic would convey the information to Goran Hadzic or to the commander of the TO as part of their agreement. It's an assumption you make, but you have no certainty about the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I assume that some decisions were made that I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Goran Hadzic comes here, we'll ask the question, but of course for that he needs to come here. All right. It's an assumption of yours, and according to you, that's the reason why Colonel Mrksic did absolutely nothing. One last question. I believe that in all the armed forces in the world, and especially in the JNA that at the time was an army with a very good reputation, I believe that in all armies in the world, officers draw up reports about events. And what about you, did you write a report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't draw up a written report, because I reported to my commander orally and I informed Major Sljivancanin about all the events in the evening. They didn't ask me to compile a written report. I think that was sufficient for that part of the event in which I participated. Had they asked me to compile a written report, I would have done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's assume that Colonel Mrksic did not agree or does not agree with what you're saying. What if he were to say that he was not informed, what would you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of Operations Group South, I think it's impossible for him not to be informed. Secondly, he changed the direction of the group. The group was supposed to go from the Vukovar barracks to Sremska Mitrovica. That was the task, and the change of direction was his decision. And all the problems later arose in the place where he transferred the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you have 50 minutes. But one moment. My fellow Judge has a number of questions to put to the witness. I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, I would like to have you explain to us a bit about the effective control over the members of the two divisions of the TO that were present at the Ovcara farm, the Petrova Gora and the Leva Supoderica, because it seems to me, in retrospect, that if what you have assumed actually turned out to be true, namely, that at some earlier points in time, there was an agreement between the government, the local government, and the commanders of the JNA forces present in the area, that the prisoners that were taken from the hospital in Vukovar and stored up in the hangar at the Ovcara farm, that these prisoners would at some point be handed over to the TO. That is the agreement that you have made an implication about. This is what you assume this must have happened. There must have been some sort of agreement between the JNA forces and the government that the prisoners could be handed over to the TO. In my understanding, Colonel, this would imply that if eventually the prisoners were handed over to the TO, then terrible things could happen to the prisoners, and the JNA, as such, could say, "Well, this was not our responsibility. We were not involved. We didn't do it." And so this is the dilemma that I see in this whole thing. So I'm coming back to you now to try and explain to us who exactly had the effective control over the TO volunteers, and am I right to assume that it was understood by the JNA that if crimes were committed by the TO members, then those crimes could not be -- then the JNA could not be held responsible for those crimes? Is that a correct understanding? What was the relationship between the TOs and the JNA leadership? And let me just remind you that in your statement, you mention at some point that the TO Petrova Gora and the Leva Supoderica were separated from the JNA and they set up their own headquarters. This is in your 2002 statement, on page 6. So already here you have an indication that there was some sort of separation, the TO was on one side and the JNA was on the other side, and maybe they cooperated, but in terms of control, it was a more complicated issue. I don't know if I have made my question clear, but I want you to explain a bit to us how things were understood at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say right away that I think that no one from the JNA knew. Had Mrksic known this would happen, I'm sure he would have acted differently. I don't think anyone assumed that a crime like the one that happened could happen. It was most probably a mistake that they let these men leave their control. Nobody thought that a group of men could liquidate 200 or 300 people. That is a very serious matter which no one paid attention to, no one took into consideration, and unfortunately it happened. Secondly, I couldn't tell you who was in command of the TO forces. All those three men had a group of their own, and as to who was the main commander, the chief commander, I really couldn't answer that question. But when Vukovar fell, I don't know whether you can see that in Mrksic's order, but when Vukovar fell and the operation was concluded, all the attached and subordinated units probably left the composition, and they started moving about freely. They no longer were responsible to us. They were no longer under our command, and there was no one in command of them. They were all free groups. There was no combat going on. And they had been under the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment all the time, but whether they left that detachment under orders, I don't know. However, their actions and their conducts show that they were not under the control of the JNA in those two or three days. And I think that the attitude with the JNA felt not responsible for the members of the TO because they were no longer part of our units. Everyone was preparing to return from Vukovar. The 82nd was to take over the area of responsibility. You had the government saying one thing and people acting in another way, and then something that none of us normal people assumed could possibly happen actually happened. I thought maybe someone might be beaten up or even there might be an individual killing, but that all of them could be killed, down to the last man, that was something that nobody assumed might happen. And I think that this irresponsibility by the top leadership, or maybe the failure of Commander Mrksic to correctly assess the situation, was responsible. They thought that the TO and the government would continue taking measures in the spirit of the law, that there would be an investigation procedure, and between Mrksic and Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, one should see who ordered the forces to be withdrawn, because that's where there is a gap, a hiatus. They withdrew their forces, and then the TO took over those people and did whatever they wanted. That is where the problem lies, in my view, the assessment of the situation. Could those people have made that assessment that they were preparing this sort of situation? Nobody could know that. I don't think those three commanders there, local commanders, knew that either. I don't think they knew that, either, that all those people would be shot. Well, anything is possible, but I don't believe it, because during the combat operations they were very good fighters, especially Leva Supoderica and Milan Lancuzanin. They contributed to our 1st Assault Detachment and helped us to be very successful in the combat on that axis, so that thanks to them -- and of course they had lived in that town. They knew it well, they knew the streets. They helped our young soldiers who came from all over the former Yugoslavia. There were Croats, Muslims, Serbs, all sorts of nationalities. There were soldiers from Croatia dying in Vukovar, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Macedonia, only not from Slovenia because Slovenia had already seceded. So it was a very complex situation, a very interesting situation, because after all that heavy fighting there was an omission at the end, and that's why this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. This has been extremely important, what you have just told us about the control in the days just following the fall of Vukovar. Just one question to clarify. The attitude of the members of the TO towards the prisoners, while they were still in the buses at the barracks, and also later on when you saw -- when you came with the second batch of prisoners to the Ovcara farm, that would seem to suggest that the members of the TO were quite aggressive. And so my question is: Was that not reported to Mrksic? I mean, Sljivancanin knew, so I agree, it seems like a paradox that Mrksic had no idea of just how bad things could go, but he would have been given information about the very aggressive attitude of the TO members, would he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did have this information, most probably from his chief of staff who was present there. I don't know whether they want to admit it. He also got information from Commander Vojnovic, from me also. He had a lot of information. And the officer who took over the first group, it says that in the report of that commander, that was a man from the Command, but nobody wants to say who he was. He was given the task of taking over my group, the first group, and he took them to Ovcara, because the company commander says that an officer came from the Command and took my group with -- of three buses to Ovcara. And I came there and they said, "You go there, too, because the commander ordered this." So the only thing that was not clear to me, because the first task was given to me by Sljivancanin to take them to the barracks and to organise transport to Mitrovica from the barracks, that was the real task I was given, and everything else later represented changes, and I think it's clear who bears the responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one short question, Witness. I'm sorry to ask about an impression rather than about a fact. Is it possible that rather than not knowing, the JNA commanders were afraid of this extreme aggressiveness of those who were the authors of this massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe they were afraid, because this was a small group of people. They were ordinary fighters, local people from Vukovar. They probably recognised some people there. You can't have a Command being afraid of a group of soldiers. I don't believe that. When I was on my own, I was willing to sacrifice my life, but I managed to prevent further violence and threw them outside. If you really want to, you can solve the problem. I believe there might be people who could be afraid, but I don't believe that the Command was afraid, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you believe that they could have been controlled, brought under control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When answering a question put by my fellow Judge, you said something which I believe is capital. You had said that before, but I was thinking about the scope of what you said, and now I grasp the scope of it better. You said that the assignment you had been given initially was to take the prisoners from the barracks and to take them to Mitrovica, Mitrovica being the place where the detainees, the prisoners, were to be detained. That was your original assignment. And mysteriously enough, the assignment was changed, and that might be the key to what happened. At least that's what you seem to say implicitly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason I reached this conclusion is the following: The decision Mrksic made at the briefing is the decision conveyed to me by Sljivancanin. That was the first decision. Had there been a second decision when the SAO government -- the government of Western Slavonia and Baranja had its session from 12.00 onwards, there might have been a change in the decision. I think this is the link, and the commander changed his decision for that reason. That's the link I can make, because the change took place when the government of the SAO Slavonia, Western Srem and Baranja had its session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like everybody, we try to understand why all these prisoners were executed, and we are seeking the reasons that may have led to that. During the fighting, the fighting lasted quite a while in Vukovar. Based on your estimates, how many JNA soldiers were killed, I mean, all included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to some estimates, from my Guards Brigade about 64 soldiers and officers were killed, and from the whole Operative Group South, about a thousand men lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding your brigade, you say that 64 soldiers and officers were killed. And regarding the Operational Group South, some thousand men, soldiers and officers, were killed. As to the TO members, the locals, as it were, reinforced with volunteers, but the locals, as far as you know, could you tell us how many were killed? Out of the thousand, how many of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't give you this information, because the personnel department keeps track of that information. I can't give you any numbers, I don't know the facts, but some were killed, yes. They were in the first lines. They were directly involved in combat, and they got killed. I can't tell you exactly how many. Some of them were killed fighting with us. Some of them were killed before we arrived. Nobody wants to talk about the casualties among the Serbian people, but there were dozens and dozens of corpses floating down the Danube like logs. I apologise to the victims, but they floated down the Danube like logs. Many people were killed in Vukovar, many Serbs who have been buried in rubbish dumps. There used to be 20.000 Serbs in Vukovar. When the combat started, 20.000 people left. Do you think they left because they were having a nice time? The paramilitary forces of Croatia, in July and August, committed such crimes in Vukovar, and this has yet to be proved. Let what Mercep did be proved. He was the greatest criminal against the Serbian people. They'll have to investigate him. We know that he was a great criminal, a terrible criminal. And there was this other man who was in charge of the HDZ. He was a former officer of ours. They know best what they did in the preparations for the massacre. Why was Vukovar empty? It was empty because the Serbs fled, and then the Croats fled, too, because they saw that there would be a war. The Croatian forces blocked our barracks, and they cut off water, bread, electricity for our soldiers, and they kept the barracks surrounded for a month. They shot at the barracks, fired at the barracks with mortars, and then those people from Croatia say that everything was really good in Vukovar. But that's why there was revenge. That's why there was anger. That's why individuals who had lost their nearest and dearest wanted to take revenge, and they came into a situation where they were able to take revenge. It's not chivalrous, it's not soldierly, but those who are under threat become blind. And if you have 10 or 15 men like that, that's very dangerous, and they will do what they did. Maybe they, themselves, will regret this, but it was a very difficult time. You know that wherever there is a war, it's something all soldiers hate. People think that soldiers like combat. No, that's the worst part of our job. And you have to understand this outpouring of hatred. I think it was created long before, and then it just came back. The debt was paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this lengthy answer, which enables us to understand things better. You mentioned a thousand soldiers, all included, but your answer prompts another question by me. As far as you know, regarding the Serbian civilian population, from what you say, how many Serb civilians were killed, empirically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think those were mostly weak, elderly people who stayed behind to look after their homes, and I think there were about a hundred Serb civilians who were killed; mostly elderly people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned crimes by paramilitary in July and August. To your knowledge, how many people did they kill, these Croatian paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to some information we have, between 300 and 400 people. Just as they are looking for their dead, so the Serbs are still looking for many of their own, and many have not been found yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You promised me an hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's not argue about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would need more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask my colleagues to know whether you can have an additional ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the topic, you have an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Provided your questions are focused on the topics of interest for the Trial Chamber, and we have just really defined the scope. We're not giving you additional time to go everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness and Mr. Seselj be asked to speak slowly, to avoid any overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. You and Mr. Seselj speak the same language, so please listen to his question, wait for a moment, and then provide the answer, because the interpreters have a hard time. So listen to the question carefully, then answer, then he'll have to wait as well. Otherwise, there's overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to ask questions which are exclusively of interest to my Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, would you please give me short answers to my questions. I have a lot to get through, so "yes" or "no" would be preferable whenever possible. As far as I know, you went to the war school or School of National Defence, as it was officially called?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you pass your general's exam?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was the topic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was the topic of your thesis?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Armed conflict as part of the armed forces, armed rebellion as part of the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you a security officer while you worked in the army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were the commander of Operative Group South in Negoslavci, and I suppose you ought to know that the Guards Brigade, already on the 18th of November, when Vukovar was liberated, started preparations for the return to Belgrade; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of those preparations for the return, did the Guards Brigade first organise having the volunteers transported back, not only those of the Serbian Radical Party but all the other volunteers, on the 18th, 19th, and 20th of November, by putting them onto buses going to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I want to say that the term "Seselj's volunteers" doesn't exist. The term is "volunteers" that we use, so those -- because it doesn't say on there who they were. So they were volunteers from Belgrade, under that heading. Now, the fact that some people say that they belong to Seselj or Vuk Draskovic or whatever, with us in the army, we don't make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Colonel, just briefly, please. My time is limited, but as far as I'm concerned, it's important to me that you said that on the 18th and 19th and 20th, they were already sent back in buses. Does that mean that the Leva Supoderica Detachment was reduced exclusively to the locals of Vukovar as a detachment of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: In 90 per cent of the cases, I assume that is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, you know that there were different types of volunteers. You've confirmed that. And do you know that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were exclusively included in the Leva Supoderica Detachment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of that, but I think from the stories I heard -- well, I don't have official information, but I assume that that would be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that on the 19th of November, Marin Bilic, Bili, and the commissioner of the Croatian government for Vukovar and Vesna Bosanac, head of the Vukovar Hospital, was brought to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they have a meeting there with General Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The then Captain and later Colonel Karanfilov, Borko Karanfilov, was that his name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Borce Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. Borce Karanfilov said before the Court in Belgrade and confirmed in the Mrksic, Radic and Sljivancanin trial that General Aleksandar Vasiljevic was at the command post at Negoslavci and that he became included, as he says, in interrogating Marin Bilic and Vesna Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if he says so, then I believe it to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Together with Vasiljevic, there was Colonel, later General Simeon Tumanov; right? He was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Vesna Bosanac already at that time had lists of persons who were in the Vukovar Hospital and that she brought that list to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see that when there are two questions in one, when the witness says, "Yes," what does he say "yes" to? Was General Tumanov with him, was he also his deputy at the same time? Is it "yes" to the deputy or to being with him. It's good to put one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When you have a complex question, we don't know what the witness answers to, to which part of it he answers, so try to put a series of questions with single questions, making the answers clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I asked you, Mr. Vukasinovic, whether you knew that Vesna Bosanac, in Negoslavci, brought with her a list of all the people who were in the Vukovar Hospital when Vukovar was liberated.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that, but I did hear that she brought the lists with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that then the list was dovetailed and coordinated with Aleksandar Vasiljevic and Simeon Tumanov with respect to the fate of those people, those who were to be taken to prisoner of war camps, those who would be sent in an ambulance to hospitals in Croatia, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We'll move on. Do you know that those talks were very lengthy, went on for a long time, and that Vesna Bosanac and Marin Bilic slept at the command post at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vesna Bosanac slept in the bed of Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic; is that true?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be a language problem, but I think this should be removed, this connotation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... that be redacted. When Colonel Pavkovic wasn't at the command post, then he was somewhere else, his room was empty, the bed was empty, the bed sheets were changed, and Vesna Bosanac slept there. So she was given the top level of accommodation. Nebojsa Pavkovic told me that, personally, and I'm in the same prison area with him here. Colonel Pavkovic was elsewhere. He wasn't sleeping at the command post in his office, but the bed sheets were changed on the bed and she was given the best possible treatment in that way. So why should that be struck from the record? I've had enough of this striking things from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your question could have raised a doubt. Well, you removed it; namely, that Colonel Pavkovic, not being there, that Ms. Bosanac was accommodated in his room. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, do you know that General Vasiljevic, on the 20th of November, took all the money that was in the Vukovar bank and took it to Belgrade? There was foreign currency to the tune of several million German marks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: What I know is the following, Dr. Seselj: What was seized in the Vukovar post office was two or three bags of dinars and that a smaller sum was in foreign currency that was seized from the volunteers members of the army, and so on. Foreign currency was in the Command, at the headquarters. I know that Major Sljivancanin handed over to Aleksandar Vasiljevic the foreign currency, and all the dinar, the money in dinar with cheques and receipts was in a [indiscernible], where Vladan [indiscernible], Voce, was a member, and Montijovic [phoen], Zoran, and this was handed over to some bank in Belgrade. I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, by law, that should be handed over to the military service of the National Bank of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Whereas it was not handed over where it was supposed to be handed over by law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you were retired, Mr. Vukasinovic, as an active colonel of the Military Security Service, you had an ID card which gave you special authority; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those powers and authorities are identical to the civilian police or the State Security Service; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you retired, did you have to give your ID back, giving you these special authorisations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I returned everything, and now I'm nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's a very important question for me.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I returned everything, and I have nothing left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've heard of a security officer Colonel Bogdan Vujic who was retired on the 1st of January, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Colonel Bogdan Vujic, when he retired on the 1st of January, 1991, did he, too, have to give back his ID card with all the authorisations vested in it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You heard that three retired colonels, Slavko Tomic, Bogdan Vujic and Bogoljub Kijanovic were reactivated, brought out of retirement, and that in official uniforms and with an official car, they arrived in Vukovar sometime in the night between the 19th and 20th of November; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it customary to bring colonels out of retirement, colonels of the Military Security Service, if some of them are over the age of 65?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for a decision of that kind to be taken -- well, I don't think it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, could it have been done without an order from the federal Minister of Defence or the federal Secretary of Defence, as the title was at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No, this couldn't have been done without decision and order of the federal Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that there was no such order to reactivate these people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are now retired and a reservist; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am retired, but I still have not received my assignment as a reserve person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How long will you be a -- when will this happen or how long will this apply for?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Sixty-five years old.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down between question and answer. It's impossible to follow at this rate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please slow down, the both of you, because once again the interpreters are telling us that they have a hard time following you and they can't translate everything. So, Mr. Seselj, if the answer is not recorded on the transcript, what you are trying to highlight is not going to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One comment. Mention was made here of someone who was over 65, but if you try to establish such a thing, then you need to produce a document to provide hard evidence. Here, there's a lot of speculation going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, notwithstanding this objection by the Prosecution, what about these three colonels who were brought out of retirement? Because of their age, they were not supposed to be brought out of retirement. It was not possible, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know how old they actually were. They looked like vital men. They didn't look that old. They were full of vitality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you can be in extremely good shape but above the age limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I assume you know that Slavko Tomic, Colonel Slavko Tomic, had been a partisan during World War II. Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the Prosecutor brought forward some other witnesses who gave us that information, and we have it in the transcript. They were Prosecution witnesses, and I don't want to mention their names because some of them filed through the courtroom under protective measures. But I'd just like to remind the Prosecutor of that. Anyway, sir, you said that it was not possible to reactivate retired colonels without an order from the federal secretary or, rather, federal Minister Veljko Kadijevic, who was the general of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, if I tell you that there are absolutely no papers relating to their reactivation even with the signature of Aleksandar Vasiljevic, would that be something you would find strange?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That would then be against the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see, against the law. Right. Now, if I tell you that during this reactivation period, that a new post was not regulated, if they were reactivated, they would have had to take up a new post with the JNA; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would that be against the law as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because when you reactivate an officer, that officer inherits the rights that he had previously. He inherits the military post and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If I tell you that during that month or two of reactivation, these three colonels were not on any salary list, would that -- payroll, would that be against the law too?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, it would be against the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If I tell you that in their military booklets, there was no record of them having been reactivated, would that be unlawful too?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And if I go on to tell you that in their personal file, dossier, there was no information about them having been reactivated, and this was established by my associates in Belgrade in direct communication with the Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, and they received information from the army too, would that be contrary to the law as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because everything had to be entered into their personal file, right, all these factors?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, even observations about their work in the field. Everything would be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If, in Sremska Mitrovica, where a camp for prisoners of war was organised in a prison there, if there was an order there that they go to Sid first and from thence to Vukovar to perform a special assignment, would it be contrary to the law that there was no written order about their departure to Sid and Vukovar on assignment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose there's an order from Aleksandar Vasiljevic, who engaged them and decided to send them. It would have to say what the basic assignment was and where they were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We established with great certainty that there's no written trace. That's already been established, and I can't tell you whose testimony confirmed that. But would it be against the law if there are no written traces of any of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, is it also against the law if they were issued an order, arrived on the 19th in the evening, in Vukovar, spent the whole night in Vukovar, and then the next day some of them were in the Vukovar hospital, some of them were in the Velepromet building and then went to Ovcara, and at least -- we know that at least two of them were at Ovcara, Slavko Tomic and Bogoljub Kijanovic. Whether Bogdan Vujic was there is a debatable point still. Anyway, but around midnight on the 20th, when the execution at Ovcara had already started, they went back to Sremska Mitrovica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're going so fast that the dispatching of three colonels has not been recorded on the transcript. If it is important that we know which colonel was at the hospital, which was at Velepromet and which was elsewhere, it has to be recorded. And if you look at the screen, you will see that it has not been recorded. We, the Trial Chamber, will not be able to use this later if it's not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, after quite a long time I have the first competent witness here, who is a military expert and a recognised, reputable officer, and had he come as a Defence witness, I would have allowed him at least three hours for testimony because he knows a great many things. Now, even if he doesn't know some things directly, he knows how to interpret them. So you must understand my haste, because I want to get through all the questions that I have to ask him within that very short hour that I've been given. But let me repeat what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We have already established here that they were in Vukovar, that Bogdan Vujic was in the Vukovar hospital, that he was at Velepromet, and that at least Slavko Tomic and Bogoljub Kijanovic were at Ovcara that night, that they were at Ovcara that night. That's been established here. Now, my question to you is this: Is it possible, after that special assignment, that they did not table a single report to their superior command, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, who was their chief? Would that be against the law if they did not report back?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, their stay at Ovcara, if that is correct, in those late hours -- well, we don't know why, it's not clear why they were there. I'm hearing that from you now; and secondly, it's absolutely against the law, because they were employed by Aleksandar Vasiljevic, a level above all of us. So without writing down observations of that kind, that would be amateurish and against the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As an officer of military security for many years, you know what the practice was in that service. Tell me, was it customary for you to go on assignment and then take a non de jure like Bogdan Vujic is mentioned everywhere in Vukovar as Colonel Branko, a pseudonym. When he interrogated prisoners at Sremska Mitrovica, once again he introduced himself as Colonel Branko. Was that usual in your service?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No. As an official person, there was no need for him to use a pseudonym. A pseudonym is only used when one is working with informers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So there was no reason for him to conceal his true identity. He should have introduced himself with his full name and first name as a JNA colonel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the general rule, to introduce himself under his real name. There was no need for him to use a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on. In addition to these three colonels, there was also another group of security officers there who had come from the 1st Military District. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was General Mile Babic there as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was General Jerko Crmaric there? He was a Croat by ethnicity and deputy commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about him. I know that he was deputy commander for logistics, and I know that occasionally we had problems with ammunition supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Did you see there at any point in time a colonel of the Military Security Service wearing an aviation uniform, who was also in charge of the transfer of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, do you know that on the 19th of November, immediately on the eve of the arrival of General Vasiljevic, Colonel Sljivancanin had received a cable from him in which General Vasiljevic ordered him to secure, as many as possible, prisoners of war who should be transferred to Sremska Mitrovica, where they were to be exchanged for a large number of JNA members who were kept prisoner by Croats?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that, and I personally saw such a cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall proceed further on immediately. Therefore, the task of the security officers was to ensure as many prisoners of war as possible and to bring them to Sremska Mitrovica, ensure their presence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the beginning of combat operations, it was our attempt, and that was the message we had received from the Command -- or, rather, from the Cabinet of the federal Defence minister, that there were many soldiers and families kept prisoner in Croatia and that we had to gather as many prisoners of war as possible in order to exchange them. And that was our task, to gather as many persons that could later be exchanged, and this is why we insisted upon that. And we took care of all of those people, preparing them for exchange, so that a large number of people, around 1.500, were in Sremska Mitrovica. We had sent them from Vukovar there in order to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Among those people that General Vasiljevic attempted to free from Croatian prisons, there was a large number of officers and civilian associates of the groups called Opera and Labrador?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: As for the associates and agents, I don't know anything about that, but I know that a large number of our officers and their families had been imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And some of them were included in these agent networks; right? You know that as much as I do.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That network had been busted completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that people from that group organised the planting of a bomb at the Jewish cemetery in Zagreb and the Jewish municipal building in order for that to be ascribed to the Tudjman regime?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I heard about it, but I don't really know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you know at least as much as I do from the press?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know as much; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, and that's quite a satisfactory answer for me as well. Now, tell me, please, the key problem here was this: You had been given an assignment to go with six buses to transport prisoners of war from the hospital to the barracks, and from there on to Sremska Mitrovica; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were shocked when, upon your return from the hospital, you saw that three buses had already been sent to Ovcara and that an order was conveyed to you that your three buses should go to Ovcara as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was not logical at all, there was absolutely no logic in it; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, no logic whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You cannot bring it into any -- you can't make sense in that, either looking at the telegram of General Vasiljevic or the practice, the standard procedure of JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's see if we can find some logic there. Was it possible for the JNA to transfer a group of prisoners, precisely 200 of them, to the civil authorities of the Serbian Autonomous Region Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Srem, when it was a well-known fact that this autonomous region was not regulated at all within the constitutional system of the Yugoslav Federation? Was it possible at all for the JNA to transfer their prisoners to these people? According to the regulations, was it possible at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: According to the regulations, the JNA should not transfer prisoners in such a way. They should have followed a procedure, if they were still within their area of responsibility, and they were. They should have taken these people to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And especially the JNA could not have transferred 200 prisoners to anyone without any paperwork. They should have received some sort of a receipt. So many prisoners were transferred, and they should have listed them, and there should have been a signature there; am I right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, because when the organs of military police and security service do their work without any influence from the Command, that's the procedure that should be in place. The military police escorts prisoners, they make up a list with the names, but it is mandatory, upon arrival to the prison, to transfer the custody of prisoners according to the list with names. This is their basic duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it one of the tasks within the Military Security Service to evacuate and to safely house prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Their main task is counter-intelligence, and what you said was the main task of the military police. And the military police, in the professional sense, was subordinated to the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I didn't say "the main task," I said "one of the main tasks," and now that I've corrected myself, would you answer in the affirmative?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is one of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. That's exactly what I said. Now, please, the mere fact that in Vukovar, after the liberation, the town headquarters or the town command was set up, is that yet another proof that the JNA still did not consider that the civilian authorities were able to carry out their normal, everyday duties in that area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this comes out of my sphere of responsibility, but if you want my personal opinion, I will tell you that, yes, it wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm asking you here now as an expert, as a colonel. Had the JNA believed that the civil authorities were able to take over all of their responsibilities and duties, then they would not have set up this town Command, the military town Command; is that right? According to the military regulation of the JNA, the town Command or the headquarters or administration of a town is only set up in a liberated town until the civilian authorities are able to take over power; am I right? You're looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the screen because I'm seeing that the interpretation is still going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, it's not interpretation. It's the transcript and the transcript is always late, so you better turn it off.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in order for us not to overlap, and we have been warned about that. That is why I'm making a pause. Yes, you're quite right. In a liberated town, in a liberated neighbourhood or area, the Command, town Command, continues to exist until all civilian authorities are established, and civilian protection services, and it is upon that -- it is only after that that the military withdraws and hands over power to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that even before the liberation of Vukovar, that the headquarters administration was set up that encompassed Ovcara and an additional two villages around Ovcara, and that Colonel Vojnovic was the commander before he became the town commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is very vague. Could Mr. Seselj give us a date, provide a document? Could he be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, what about this Colonel Vojnovic who became the town commander; when was it, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj [as interpreted], I said before the liberation of Vukovar, before the 18th of November. Now, as to precise date, is it important? It was perhaps on the 17th, on the 12th. I don't know. What do I care? But he was -- he held the post of the commander of the area, including Ovcara, and that's important for me. And it was only upon the order of Mrksic that he was appointed commander of the town of Vukovar. It was on the 22nd or 23rd of November; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. The then Colonel Vojnovic, the commander of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade, received an area of responsibility encompassing Ovcara, Jakobovac, Grabovo, and I'm not sure about Sutin. In that area of responsibility, he had his subordinate units, commands or battalions and so on, and his main command post would have been in Jakobovac, in Grabovo, in Sutin, it makes no difference, but he's responsible for that entire area. That's his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the command of Colonel Vojnovic was housed in a so-called yellow house in the immediate vicinity of Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am familiar with this yellow house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please turn off the transcript. You're just using up my time by waiting for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, what you're saying needs to be translated, but also to be transcribed. The witness is right. You should wait.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how am I to manage to do everything in this one hour? I don't know, myself, Ms. Lattanzi. I will do my best, but I don't know if I will succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you keep making comments about what everyone says, including what the Judges say, I'm not surprised that you don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It seems that I'm my own worst enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Vukasinovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. I do not exactly know what your point is, what you are trying to establish. Earlier on, you mentioned three colonels who were reactivated. This seemed to be rather interesting. I was wondering why such a thing happened. But you left that aside, and now you're moving on to a different topic. You may raise this matter again at a later stage, but if that's not the case, then I'm going to ask you, what was the point of mentioning these three colonels in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm receiving English interpretation. It seems like they are trying to provoke me by translating my own words for me into English. So I have this concept for my cross-examination, and it will make sense for you at the end. Please trust me, that I will do it perfectly, if I manage to achieve it within this short space of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then we'll wait to see what happens, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, is it true that the government of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem was a mere political improvisation and that it did not have a developed judicial system at the time, judicial apparatus?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that that government, even had it wanted, even had it been entrusted with it, was unable to organise regular trials, proper trials, for these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: My opinion, and these are just my impressions, in that early period of time, when we still hadn't left and they still hadn't established their organs of authority, I think it wasn't possible at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Vukasinovic, you said earlier something that surprised me, when Vukovar was liberated, that these TO units left immediately from the composition of the Guards Brigade. However, the OTP has an order, and this was shown to us here by the OTP expert --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to make it very clear that the witness said that it was likely. If Mr. Seselj quotes the witness, he should be very specific. He said "probably." Page 52, line 20 of the transcript, "probably."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree with this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said "probably." I wasn't sure. I said that because I saw them around, moving about without any orders, without any commands, that they had nothing to do, and this is how I came to that conclusion. It seemed like they came out of the composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But their numbers were reduced with the departure of volunteers so that none of those units could have had more than 30 to 40 men; am I right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's precisely what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. There was a military expert of the OTP here who brought with him a document, an order of Colonel Mrksic to the effect that the TO units were resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade. Was that logical, was that in accordance with the regulations in situations where the Guards Brigade was leaving Vukovar and its responsibilities were being taken over by the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, Colonel Vojnovic, at the time he was lieutenant colonel, was appointed commander of Vukovar by way of an order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm reluctant to interrupt Mr. Seselj, but the document is document P41. It has a date. Could that document be shown to the witness, because we do not know exactly what you are talking about at this moment. It's just a suggestion I'm making to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have concluded that. You have the document in evidence, and why do we need to bother ourselves with it now? It's marginal for my purposes here, and why would you interrupt my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the document has been admitted. All right. But to avoid any speculation by the Judges with respect to this document, you should have said, "We have document or exhibit P41," saying such-and-such thing, and then you would have put your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't have a single assistant. How do you expect me to look up all those numbers? You see that I'm absolutely swamped with papers. I am absolutely unable to do all that by myself, and I'm going directly to the heart of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, my next question: Everybody in Vukovar knew that a group of prisoners had been taken to Ovcara. Foreign journalists saw that. There were also foreign observers there. Even Vance happened to be in Vukovar on that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Cyrus Vance was in Vukovar on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. And then between the 20th and the 21st, it was then that the execution was carried out during the night?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The entire Vukovar knew that the prisoners had been executed. The rumours spread out immediately; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How was it possible that the new commander of Vukovar, Colonel Vujovic, did nothing to investigate this case of execution? He did absolutely nothing, and he was the only one responsible to do that. Wasn't his conduct unlawful?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that he was the town commander and also the commander of the area where this happened, I think he was the most responsible person to report on that and take measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you agree that he did not take any measures?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Under his command, sanitization of the terrain in the area of Vukovar was carried out. Corpses of people who had been killed were collected. People were excavated from improvised burial sites, and all these dead were systematically buried at the Vukovar cemetery; is that correct? And this refers to over 900 people. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. And the sanitization of the terrain covered all the locations where people who had been killed were temporarily buried, except for this mass grave at Ovcara. Nobody even approached it. Is that illegal?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's unlawful if the war theatre is not sanitised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You, yourself, said during the examination-in-chief that your commander, Colonel Mrksic, seemed odd to you when you told him what had happened at Ovcara. This means that he did not respond immediately in the way you expected him to, knowing him well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does not that mean that at that time, there was a far higher authority than Colonel Mrksic around? Am I right in saying that all you security officers, and not just officers -- or, rather, not just security officers, but all the officers, view General Vasiljevic with a kind of awe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say it that way. Maybe some did, but we lower-ranking officers, ops officers, were not afraid of General Vasiljevic. And I did find Colonel Mrksic's behaviour odd. I knew him as a very capable officer and I thought he should have dealt with this straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. The very fact that the prisoners were shot between the 20th and the 21st of November and that the first investigations were started in Belgrade only in 1998, when an affair began and foreigners exhumed the mass grave in 1996, and they were only assisted by Croatian and Serbian pathologists and experts in forensic medicine, does that mean that somebody intentionally tried to conceal the crime at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It calls for speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The secrecy, the very fact that nobody did anything, is very illustrative, and it shows that there was some sort of invisible secret activities aimed at concealing this. Who was responsible for that, I don't know, but nobody wanted to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So somebody wanted to cover this up at any price. That's not speculation, is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was evident that there were attempts to cover it up. It was a very serious matter, and it would lead to people being held responsible. Well, the number of people who were killed was 200, so -- well, the policy was to keep this quiet. I don't know who was responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when, finally, under public pressure, investigations were started under the leadership of General Gojovic, who was then a colonel, was it clear that General Gojovic is trying to prevent, by every possible means, the names of General Vasiljevic and General Simeon Tumanov being mentioned in that context, was that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I made a statement under my first and last name. I was not aware of that. But later on, I made the statement in the Security Administration, and Colonel Branko -- I can't remember his last name -- insisted, when I was giving my statement to him, that there was just Sljivancanin and I there. And I said, "No, no, no, you can't say that. If we are telling the truth, then you have to say who was there, who was in charge, who was aware of what was going on." But the policy was to blame Sljivancanin and me for everything, only us and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, was it not clear that they sacrificed --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Gajic, I remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That it was decided at a higher level to sacrifice Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. You're so fast, Mr. Seselj, that I find it hard to grasp it all. What you say may be important, but you move from one topic to the next very quickly. Especially, the issue of the date is very important. As I understand it, Colonel Branko interviewed you, Witness, and if I understand properly, because Mr. Seselj is so fast, you really have to read between the lines. Colonel Branko seemed to suggest to you, as it were, for you to bear the responsibility, and for you and Sljivancanin to accept the responsibility. But you don't agree or you didn't agree, and you said so to Colonel Branko. Is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I believe you added this: They then decided to sacrifice Colonel Mrksic, or something to the effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to talk about the policy of sacrificing someone, but about uncovering the truth, who did what. You can't reduce it all to Sljivancanin or Vukasinovic, when you have to go from the top to the bottom all the way down the chain. That's the procedure, to see from the very top to the very bottom, the last soldier at Ovcara, who did what, who saw what, who knew what, who took what measures, and then the situation would be clear. If we exclude this one and that one, it would turn out that Sljivancanin thought all this up by himself and did it all by himself, and that's nothing to do with reality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time have I got left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Precisely, I was about to tell you. Twenty-four minutes left, but we have to have a break. It might be best to have a break now. Judge Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the date of this interview with Colonel Branko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand. There was an interruption, there was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asking about the date of this interview with Colonel Branko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was in November 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That means that Colonel Bogdan Vujic was engaged in 1996 in covering up the crime at Ovcara. Why would he be talking to you, an active duty officer, as a retired officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: On his return from Vukovar, he was sent back into retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about Branko Gajic now.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, all right, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break. We shall resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, as an officer of the Military Security Service, I assume that throughout all that time, you were aware that there were many foreign intelligence agents in the Vukovar area posing as humanitarian workers, international representatives, and so on.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my chief of service had that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As these foreign intelligence agents had formal cover, they had the status of humanitarian workers or international representatives, you were unable to put a stop to their activities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the counter-intelligence protection of units has to cover that segment also, the fight against the intelligence work of the other side, but we based ourselves more on the intelligence activities of the Croatian paramilitary forces because they were a bigger threat to our forces than the foreign intelligence agents. I don't think they were really a threat, although the information they gathered was probably significant for them. But our task was to deal with Vukovar, and our operation, and all the problems that had to do with threats to our units, our commands, our facilities and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they were not your priority. However, their intelligence reports had major political consequences through the behaviour of Western governments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't read these intelligence reports, so I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on, then. As an intelligence officer, are you aware that the Croatian paramilitary forces, sometime in October 1991, killed over 150 Serb civilians in the Gospic area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that, because one of our officers, Toma Strelja [phoen], was taken prisoner. He had been the garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me, are you aware that the International Public heard about this crime and that some Western governments which were already on the point of deciding to recognise Croatian independence were -- had second thoughts because of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on. I won't insist. If I tell you that according to all the information I have, which I believe are now beyond dispute, 207 war prisoners were brought to Ovcara, 7 were released, and precisely 200 were shot, as an intelligence officer, do you find this figure of precisely 200 people shot telling? It's as if somebody had issued an order, "Shoot 200," and those who did the shooting didn't want to shoot a single man more than 200, and then they let these 7 go?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Calls for speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, precisely 200. The Chamber knows this, the Prosecutor knows this, and I do. So precisely 200 were shot and 7 were released. Those are indisputable facts.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I know how many I transported, more or less. But how many were shot, I don't know. The first 15 were released, and now this number of 7 is turning up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the ones you released from the barracks, but 7 were let go from Ovcara. We have Croatian experts here and they confirmed this. Nobody cast doubt on it. The papers -- the documents show that this is correct, the forensic reports and so on, in which Serbs also participated. So the number of 200 is beyond dispute, but is it telling? Tell me, as an intelligence officer, does it say something to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: It's a large number. To kill 200 people is really dreadful. But the fact that it's a round number, 200, really is telling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that Croatian war prisoners, located in Sremska Mitrovica, and Serbs imprisoned in Croatian prisons, including officers and civilians involved in the Opera and Labrador intelligence networks, were exchanged in early December, and that Aleksandar Vasiljevic personally, with a group of Croat prisoners, and Vesna Bosanac, travelled by plane to Zagreb Airport, that Aleksandar Vasiljevic personally flew to Zagreb, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're not aware of that. Well -- but I also hope that this is also not challenged by the OTP, because they have this information. Mr. Vukasinovic, in one place in your statement you say that not a single member of the JNA took part directly in the crime at Ovcara. Unfortunately, I have to challenge this. There was at least one. His name was Spasoje Petkovic, known as Stuka. Have you heard of him? He was a conscript, serving his regular military term in the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: When I made this statement, I was convinced of this. However, as you can see, there is always an exception. This one regular soldier serving under Captain Radic managed to get away and take part in this. As you say, that name didn't mean anything to me. That's his problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, now I'll tell you briefly what I have finally discovered. And then you and Their Honours will understand what all these previous questions were for. The Croats killed civilians in Gospic. There was a danger that the Western forces would not recognise Croatia because of this crime. On the other hand, Aleksandar Vasiljevic was doing his level best to have an exchange and to get people released from prison who could compromise him directly because of the Opera and Labrador affair. The Croats put a condition to him. They said, "Shoot 200 Croat prisoners so that we can have a propaganda means against the Serbs." Maybe they didn't explain it that far. And he agreed with Vesna Bosanac which Croats from Vukovar Hospital would be easiest to sacrifice. They were often criminals, poor people, people who they thought, according to their criteria, were of least value, so that prisoners were shot. Western intelligence agents and journalists immediately got this information out. The propaganda against the Serb people was achieved, the goal was achieved, and Vasiljevic went to Zagreb personally to collect his associates from the Opera operation. What do you think of my conclusion, as an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness answers, I'd like to say that this is a compound question, a speculative one, and that the Defence has to establish facts and then to present arguments, but only in their closing brief. So hence my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was put to you, Witness. What do you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very complex question. I agree there with the Prosecutor. However, during that period of time, when I was engaged, my level was a low one. Later on I didn't deal with problems of that kind, so that your assessment and your thoughts on the matter, as far as the involvement of Aleksandar Vasiljevic is concerned, that that was possible, I really can't say "yes" or "no." I would like to remain neutral, because I can't actually say, I can't link it all up together. I fully recognise you and your image and your position, so let it remain there, but I can't confirm it myself in the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. That's a satisfactory answer as well. I'll accept that, because judging by everything, you're a very proper and correct witness.
